analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to disclose funded studies in rule comments, fines false corporate comments, and creates a public advocate for rulemaking.
analysis.headline: Backed by 85 House members, the Stop Corporate Capture Act never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite how federal agencies write the rules that implement laws on health, safety, wages, and the environment. Companies submitting studies in rule comments would have to disclose who funded them, public companies caught making false statements in comments would face fines starting at $250,000, and a new Public Advocate inside the White House budget office would help ordinary people navigate and influence rulemaking. It would also bar industry from negotiated rulemaking, put a 60-day clock on White House review of rules, require agencies to answer petitions with 100,000 signatures, and let agencies reinstate rules Congress voted to kill.
analysis.who_benefits: People who depend on federal rules — air and water quality, workplace safety, food, drugs, consumer finance — would get a more open process where industry-funded research and behind-the-scenes edits are disclosed, false corporate comments are punished, and agencies must respond to large public petitions. Individual commenters, public interest groups, and consumer, labor, and environmental organizations would gain support from the new Public Advocate, and agencies would regain the ability to reinstate rules stripped under the Congressional Review Act.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who rely on federal safety rules

how_it_helps.text: Any person submitting a scientific, economic, or technical study in a rule comment would have to disclose who funded it, how much they were paid, whether a regulated party reviewed or revised it, and any financial ties between the researchers and parties affected by the rule — and agencies would have to flag publicly when a study is at least 10% funded by a regulated entity.

Public companies filing false or misleading rule comments would face civil penalties of at least $250,000 for a first violation and at least $1 million for each later violation, and violating comments could be thrown out of the record.

A new Office of the Public Advocate, led by a Senate-confirmed National Public Advocate, would help individuals participate in rulemaking, write rules information in plain, multilingual language, partner with community organizations, and produce social-equity assessments of proposed rules within 30 days on request.

White House (OIRA) review of significant rules would be capped at 60 days, with one 60-day extension, and agencies could publish rules if review ran past the deadline; agencies would also have to disclose publicly every change made between draft and final rules and whether White House or other officials prompted them.

Agencies would have to respond in writing within 60 days to any rulemaking petition gathering more than 100,000 signatures, and could reinstate rules rescinded by Congressional Review Act resolutions — immediately during a one-year window, and after that through ordinary notice-and-comment rulemaking.

The bill would write the Chevron doctrine into statute — courts would have to defer to an agency's reasonable reading of a law Congress left ambiguous — protecting agency expertise from judicial second-guessing, and it would require cost-benefit analyses to count nonquantifiable public benefits and prioritize rules that benefit the public.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations and industry groups that dominate the rulemaking comment process would bear new disclosure obligations, fines of $250,000 to $1 million for knowingly false comments, public flagging of conflicts of interest, and the loss of a seat in negotiated rulemaking. The White House regulatory review office (OIRA) would lose its power to hold rules indefinitely. Taxpayers would fund the new Office of the Public Advocate, and agencies would absorb compliance costs for expanded notification, docket, and disclosure duties.

drawbacks.text: Writing the Chevron doctrine into statute with no exception for major or consequential rules would lock in broad judicial deference to agencies of either party, which defenders of judicial oversight argue weakens the courts' check on executive power.

The bill limits negotiated rulemaking committees to federal, state, local, and tribal governments, striking references to other affected participants including residents of rural areas — so it removes not only industry but also some affected public groups from the negotiating table.

The Office of the Public Advocate would sit inside the Office of Management and Budget — the same office whose regulatory review division the bill curbs — and its head would be appointed by the President, so the advocate's independence would depend entirely on whoever held the White House.

The penalties and mandatory funding disclosures could deter some businesses and groups from filing comments at all rather than risk a fine or public conflict flagging, reducing the range of input agencies hear.

Letting agencies reinstate rules that Congress voted to nullify under the Congressional Review Act bypasses a disapproval mechanism Congress created, a separation-of-powers objection even from people who dislike the CRA itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aimed squarely at a real asymmetry: industries file the bulk of substantive rulemaking comments, often citing research they funded themselves, while ordinary people rarely engage at all. Funding disclosure, public conflict flags, and penalties for false corporate comments attack that asymmetry directly, and the Public Advocate, petition-response requirement, and OIRA deadlines would make the process more reachable and faster. The costs are real but moderate: a new office, compliance burdens on filers, and a deference rule that cuts both ways — it would have shielded protective rules from deregulatory courts, but also shielded any agency's overreach. Timing mattered: the Supreme Court overruled the Chevron doctrine in Loper Bright v. Raimondo in June 2024 while this bill sat in committee, so enacting it afterward would have partially reversed that ruling. On balance, this is a well-aimed transparency bill whose main weakness is that its strongest tools (Chevron codification, CRA reinstatement) depend on which party controls the White House.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, neither ever took it up, and the two-year Congress ended with no markup and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on March 9, 2023, joined by nine original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Oversight and Accountability Committee.
It attracted 84 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, over the course of the Congress.
No committee ever held a markup or vote, the bill never came to the House floor, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill dead in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies and industry groups whose rulemaking comments would have faced funding disclosure, public conflict flags, and six- and seven-figure penalties for false statements are better off, since the comment process now runs as it did before; House Republican committee chairs also avoided a contested vote on an 85-cosponsor bill.

industries.industry: Regulated industries filing rulemaking comments (pharmaceutical, chemical, energy, financial and other corporations)
industries.note: These companies fund most expert studies cited in rule comments. The bill would force them to disclose funding, reviewers, and financial ties, flag studies with 10% or more regulated-party funding, and pay fines starting at $250,000 for knowing false statements — ending a channel through which regulated parties shape the rules that bind them.

Their core product — anonymized, industry-funded technical comments and back-channel influence over draft rules — would become public. Agencies would have to disclose every change made after White House review and who prompted it, and withdrawn rules would need a public explanation.

industries.industry: Industry participants in negotiated rulemaking committees
industries.note: Negotiated rulemaking, where affected parties draft rules together, would be limited to government entities, taking industry (and some affected public groups, such as rural residents) out of the room. Industry loses a seat at the table; the note cuts both ways for the public.

OIRA's centralized review of significant rules would face a hard 60-day clock, mandatory written justification for delays, and public disclosure of changes requested during review — curbing the presidency's power to quietly shape or stall rules regardless of which party holds it.
